title: Chananya son of Chizkiya son of Garon (or Gurion)

paragraphs: Hananiah son of Hezekiah son of Garon or Gurion. Hyman describes him as the leading figure of the generation in the time of Hillel and Shammai, through whom there remained to us, as a remnant, the book of Ezekiel and Megillat Taanit. As in Shabbat 13b: Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav: Truly, that man is remembered for good, and Hananiah son of Hezekiah is his name, for were it not for him the book of Ezekiel would have been hidden away — what did he do? They brought up three hundred jars of oil, and he sat in an upper chamber and expounded it. And so it is in Chagigah 13,

and in Menachot 45, it reads 'Hanina son of Hezekiah'. And in Shabbat 13b: Who wrote Megillat Taanit? They said: Hananiah son of Hezekiah and his company, who cherished troubles; and at the end of Megillat Taanit (שר׳ [printed abbreviation retained; expansion uncertain]) [it says that] Eleazar son of Hanania son of Hezekiah son of Garon wrote it. Hyman concludes: Without doubt both are true, that the father and his son wrote the scroll. And in Shabbat chapter 1, mishnah 4: And these are among the halakhot that they stated in the upper chambers of Hananiah ben Hezekiah ben Gurion

(and in the Gemara there, 13a, 'ben Garon') when they went up to visit him: they counted votes, and Beit Shammai outnumbered Beit Hillel, and eighteen matters they decreed on that day. And in Chagigah 13a: An incident with a certain child — who was contemplating the hashmal, and fire came out of the hashmal and burned him — Hananiah ben Hezekiah said to him: If this one was wise, is everyone wise? And Eleazar his son is mentioned many times, as explained

notes.text: Hyman reports Garon/Gurion and Chananya/Chanina forms and concludes that father and son jointly composed Megillat Taanit. That conclusion remains his; the closing attribution and bibliographical function of שר׳ still need a matching version.

Chagigah13a in the named William Davidson text has the rhetorical response If this one was wise, is everyone wise? The question challenges the inference from one child’s ability; it does not assert universal wisdom.

The whole consulted Shabbat 13b passages name Hananiah and his company as writers of Megillat Taanit, retain their cherishing troubles, and give the upper chamber and three hundred jars of oil. The whole Menachot 45a passage instead has Hanina son of Hezekiah; the supplied unsided citation 45 remains as supplied. The whole Chagigah 13a child passage gives a rhetorical question, not an assertion that everyone is wise, and says to them beside Hyman’s to him. The supplied abridgments are not expanded. Hyman’s statement about the leading figure of Hillel and Shammai’s generation remains his chronological description. His WITHOUT DOUBT conclusion that BOTH father and son wrote the scroll retains its confident force as his argument. The exact final Megillat Taanit witness naming Eleazar has not been independently collated: the two whole closing paragraphs consulted in the digital Warsaw 1874 Adar text do not contain it, which is not evidence of absence elsewhere. The literal שר׳ remains unresolved; the older scholion expansion is not newly endorsed. Garon/Gurion and Hananiah/Hanina/Hanania forms remain distinct, and the final son’s cross-reference is not a new identity admission. All Hebrew and current notes remain unchanged.
